transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, it's... it's a lot of things, really, but I guess the main thing that finally made me make the appointment is that my eating has just gotten so completely off track. I mean, it's not like I was ever a huge eater, but lately, some days I barely get down a cup of coffee and maybe a granola bar before I have to head in for a shift at the clinic. And working in healthcare support, you know, you're on your feet all day, lifting patients, running around, you need energy. But I just look at food and I can't even... I don't want it. It's like the thought of chewing and swallowing is just too much effort. And the thing is, I've noticed my scrubs, the blue ones I always wear on Tuesdays, they've been hanging so loose on me lately. I actually had to pull the drawstring tight the other day just to keep the pants up, and I haven't been trying to lose weight at all. I haven't changed my routine, I haven't been to the gym in months, but the weight is just falling off because I'm basically running on fumes and caffeine most days. It's just... it's not right, you know? I should be eating. I know I should be eating. But I just can't seem to make myself do it.
Are you avoiding food because you want to lose weight or because you’re worried about gaining weight?

No, no, definitely not. Like I was just saying, I haven't been trying to lose weight whatsoever. I mean, I'm a 46-year-old guy working in healthcare support, I'm not exactly worried about having a beach body or fitting into skinny jeans or anything like that. It's really just that... well, exactly what brought me in today, my eating has just gotten so completely off track. Some days I barely get down that cup of coffee and a single granola bar before a shift, and it has absolutely nothing to do with wanting to be thin or being scared of gaining a few pounds. 

If anything, seeing my scrubs hanging so loose on me is actually kind of stressing me out. It bothers me because I know my body needs fuel. When you're helping transfer patients from a bed to a wheelchair, you need your core strength, you need calories. But the appetite just isn't there at all. It's like my stomach is just turned off. The actual mechanics of eating—getting the food out of the fridge, putting it on a plate, the chewing, the swallowing—it all just feels like climbing a mountain right now. So, no, there's no diet plan happening here, the weight is just falling off completely by accident because I just can't bring myself to care about food.
Have you been feeling down or depressed?

Yeah... yeah, I have. It's actually really bad lately. It's like... well, most mornings I wake up with this heavy, hollow feeling, just sitting right in the center of my chest. It's like the day is already completely ruined before I even swing my legs out of bed, before I even put on my badge for work. And it's not just a passing thing, you know? It's this deep, sinking feeling that just drags me down. I'll just lie there staring at the ceiling, thinking about the shift ahead, thinking about the alarms going off and the call lights and the charting, and it all just feels so pointless and exhausting. 

I used to actually like my job. I liked talking to the patients, helping them get comfortable, feeling like I was doing something useful. But now? Now it's just this massive weight. I drag myself to the shower, and the water just feels... I don't know, dull? Like I can't even enjoy a hot shower anymore. And then I'm standing in the kitchen, looking at the coffee maker, and that hollow feeling just spreads out to my arms and legs, making everything feel like it's made of lead. It's just this constant, dark cloud, and it doesn't matter if it's a sunny day or if one of the nurses brings in donuts for the breakroom, which usually cheers people up. I just feel so incredibly down, so drained of any kind of joy or motivation, just right from the second I open my eyes. It's exhausting just trying to pretend I'm okay when I'm clocking in.
Have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living or that you’d be better off dead?

I mean... yeah. It's hard to say out loud, but yeah, I have. Like I was just saying about those mornings, when I'm just lying there staring at the ceiling? When that alarm goes off at 5:15 AM, it's this harsh buzzing sound, and my very first thought, before I even open my eyes or reach over to hit the snooze button, is just... I just catch myself wishing I simply wouldn't wake up. 

I want to be completely clear about this, because working in the clinic, I know the protocols and I know what you have to ask—I haven't made a plan to hurt myself or anything like that. I'm not sitting at home figuring out ways to end it, I don't have anything dangerous stockpiled. It's not an active thing where I'm trying to make it happen. But... it's just this constant, exhausting thought in the back of my mind that it would just be so much easier if I disappeared. 

It's almost like a fantasy, you know? Just evaporating. Fading out into the background. Like, what if I just went to sleep on a Tuesday and the world just kept turning, the clinic kept running, the patients got transferred, but I just didn't have to be a part of it anymore? It would just be so much easier than carrying this heavy feeling around all day. No more struggling to force down a granola bar, no more dragging my feet down the linoleum hallways, no more of this massive weight. And then I feel guilty for even thinking it, because I see patients every day who are fighting so hard just to recover, just to get back to their lives, and here I am, and all I can think about is how nice it would be to just cease to exist. Just slip away quietly. It's not that I want to violently die, exactly, it's just that being alive right now feels like this endless, impossible chore, and disappearing just sounds like... relief.
How long have you been feeling this down most days?

Well, it's... it's been a really long time. I mean, the really steady, heavy part of it, that constant feeling of just being totally drained and having zero interest in anything—even the things I used to actually enjoy, like watching the game on Sundays or just going for a walk—that really settled in, I'd say, about a year and four months ago. 

I remember it pretty clearly because it was right around the time the clinic was doing our annual flu shot drive the year before last, and usually I'm the one joking around with the staff, trying to make the line move faster, you know, keeping morale up. But I just couldn't do it. I just felt this wall come down. And since then, for the last sixteen months or so, it's just been this relentless slog. 

Day in, day out, month after month. The seasons changed, the holidays came and went—Thanksgiving, Christmas, all of it—and I just felt completely disconnected from all of it. Like I was watching it happen through a dirty window. So yeah, roughly a year and four months of just... this. Just waking up every single day with that lead weight in my chest, wondering how I'm going to make it through another shift, another week, another month of feeling completely hollowed out. It hasn't let up. Not really. Not for a year and four months.
Before this current 16-month stretch, was there ever another period in your life when you felt depressed like this for at least two weeks?

No, I... I really don't think so. I mean, I've thought about this a lot, actually, because when you feel this bad for this long, you start trying to trace it back, you know? You start going through your whole life like a filing cabinet, pulling out memories and trying to see if there was a pattern you missed. I remember being a teenager and having those angsty phases, like everyone does, where you think nobody understands you and you stay in your room listening to music. And then in my twenties, when I was in school getting my associate's degree, there were definitely stressful times. I remember during my finals for my anatomy class, I was so stressed I barely slept for a week, and I felt pretty miserable then, but it was just stress, you know? It wasn't this... this heavy, dark, completely empty feeling. 

Even when things were tough—like when I started at the clinic and the learning curve was so steep, or when my dad passed away about ten years ago. That was incredibly sad, obviously, and I grieved, but it felt like normal grief. It didn't feel like this. I could still laugh at a memory of him, I could still eventually enjoy a meal or look forward to the weekend. I wasn't just dragging myself through every single minute of the day feeling like a ghost. So, no, before this last year and four months, I've never had a stretch like this. I've never felt this completely, utterly defeated for two weeks, or even a few days, let alone sixteen months. This is... this is entirely new territory for me, and it's just so foreign compared to how I used to be. I used to be the guy who could always find a silver lining, and now... now I just can't remember what that even felt like. But yeah, to answer your question, no, nothing like this before.
